summary: Extends the Presence Information Data Format, the XML format for describing whether someone is available, so that a presence document can carry only part of the information. Plain PIDF always carries everything, which wastes bandwidth on slow or high-latency links. Partial presence documents send just what has changed.

plainLanguage.summary: Telling friends you are free is easy, but resending your whole profile every time is a waste. This lets you send just the one thing that changed, like your status, saving data on slow connections.

questions: how do pidf diff updates work
subtitle: A way to send only the changed parts of a presence document instead of the whole thing every time.

tldr.problem: A plain PIDF presence document must always carry all the presence information available for the presentity, which wastes bandwidth on low-bandwidth, high-latency links.
tldr.mechanism: A new MIME type, application/pidf-diff+xml, carries either a full document (pidf-full root) or a partial one (pidf-diff root) that applies add, replace and remove patch operations to the receiver's cached copy.
tldr.outcome: Watchers can receive just the changes, and endpoints that do not understand the new type keep using application/pidf+xml.

today: RFC 5262 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2008. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Partial Presence
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), from RFC 3863, is the baseline XML format for describing presence. One of its characteristics is that a document always carries all the presence information available for the presentity. Where low-bandwidth and high-latency links exist, it is often better to limit what crosses the network.

This RFC introduces the MIME type application/pidf-diff+xml, which transports either only the changed parts or the full PIDF-based information. The root element tells the receiver which one it got. A note in the RFC points out that a separate type lets applications negotiate support for partial updates using the Accept header, and that no new type would have been needed had PIDF been designed for partial updates from the start.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending your whole profile each time is slow on a weak connection. This idea is to send only what changed.

sections.title: Full and Partial Documents
sections.content:
The RFC uses the vocabulary of RFC 2778 and defines two terms. A full presence document contains all the presentity's presence information that is available to a particular watcher. A partial presence document represents a fragment of the full one.

A partial document can only be understood in the context of the full document: it modifies a cached copy of the full presence document held by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: A full document is the whole page. A partial one is a sticky note that only makes sense if you already have the page.

sections.title: Structure of PIDF Diff Documents
sections.content:
The XML Schema imports the PIDF schema, so full content can be carried with an added version attribute. In that case the root element is <pidf-full>, and its content is exactly what application/pidf+xml would have carried. The schema also allows <presence> as a root, but applications using this format must not use it.

When only changes are sent, the model of the XML patch operations in RFC 5261 is used and the root is <pidf-diff>. The elements <add>, <replace> and <remove> change the cached copy: add inserts new content, replace updates, and remove deletes existing content.

The XML document MUST be well formed and SHOULD be valid. The namespace URN for the elements defined here is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf-diff.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of envelope: one holding the whole page, and one holding instructions like add this, change that, remove this.

sections.title: Version, Entity and Usage
sections.content:
Both root elements MAY carry a version attribute, a sequence number incremented by one between subsequent updates. Receivers can use it to order documents and to detect lost updates, which supports the "state delta" processing described in RFC 3265. One counter is kept across both <pidf-full> and <pidf-diff> documents.

The <pidf-diff> element MAY also carry an entity attribute. If present, it holds a presentity URI that MUST equal the entity value of the <presence> element in RFC 3863.

A partial document SHOULD contain only the elements or attributes that changed. When there are a lot of changes, the full document can be sent instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Each update gets the next number, like page numbers, so you can tell if you missed one.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives a full document with a presentity pres:someone@example.com at version 567. It then shows a <pidf-diff> at version 568 that adds a new tuple before the note element, replaces a tuple's basic status text with open, removes a busy activity, and replaces a contact priority attribute with 0.7. A final listing shows the local composition after applying the patches.

Each operation uses a sel attribute holding a selector that points at the part of the cached document to change.
sections.plainLanguage: The example starts with a full page, sends a short list of edits, and shows the page after the edits are done.

sections.title: Interoperability
sections.content:
Systems compliant with the Common Profile for Presence (CPP) cannot use this specification by default, but the RFC says this causes no interoperability problems: all endpoints and gateways must support the default type application/pidf+xml anyway. A party that does not understand this specification simply does not use it.

In SIMPLE-based systems, use of the new type is negotiated with SIP content type negotiation, as specified in partial notification (RFC 5263).
sections.plainLanguage: If someone does not understand the short notes, everyone just falls back to sending the whole page, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security and Error Handling
sections.content:
All security considerations of PIDF in RFC 3863 apply unchanged, because presence information may be highly sensitive. The protocol SHOULD provide authorization policies on what presence information can be given to which watchers, and when, see RFC 5025.

For errors, this document defines no new error elements. Errors from RFC 5261 may be used, and incorrect version or entity content MAY be indicated by the <invalid-attribute-value> error element. UTF-8 is the recommended encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Where you are and what you are doing is private, so only the right people should see it. If something in a note is wrong, the receiver can say so.
